intro: Two hundred years ago, a small cut could kill you, surgery meant terrible pain, and no one knew that tiny living germs cause many diseases. Doctors blamed bad air. Then, one careful test at a time, people began to find the real causes. A country doctor tried cowpox. A London doctor mapped a neighborhood. A chemist looked at spoiled wine under a microscope.

In this unit you will follow those discoveries, from Jenner's first vaccine in 1796 to penicillin, insulin, the polio vaccine and the shape of DNA in the 1900s. You will see how clean water, sewers and safe food, including work in Chicago and Peoria, helped people live about thirty years longer.

By the end, you will be able to explain germ theory, tell how vaccines and antibiotics work and how they differ, read simple health data, and describe how scientists change their minds when the evidence is strong.
bigQuestion: How did finding the true causes of disease change medicine and help people live longer?

title: The Germ Revolution

chapters.title: Vaccines, Germs and Clean Surgery
chapters.bigQuestion: How did careful observation and testing show that tiny living germs cause many diseases?

story.title: The Pump on Broad Street
story.kicker: A London doctor follows the deaths street by street and finds the water pump at the center.
paragraphs: Late in the summer of 1854, cholera struck the Soho neighborhood of London. Within a few days, hundreds of people were sick. Cholera caused terrible diarrhea, and many people died within a day. Families fled. Shops closed. Most doctors blamed a bad smell in the air, which they called miasma.

Dr. John Snow did not agree. He had studied cholera in earlier outbreaks. He thought something in the drinking water carried the illness. So he walked the streets, knocked on doors and wrote down where each person who died had lived and where they got their water.

The pattern was clear. The deaths clustered around one public pump on Broad Street. Some people far away had died too, but many of them had walked to that pump because they liked its water. Workers at a nearby brewery, who drank beer made on site, mostly stayed well.

Snow showed his evidence to the local leaders. On September 8, 1854, they agreed to remove the handle from the pump, so no one could use it. The outbreak was already slowing by then, and Snow said so himself. But his map and his careful counting changed how people study disease. Today he is often called a father of epidemiology.
story.think: Snow did not see a germ. What kind of evidence did he use instead, and why was it convincing?

lessons.title: Jenner and Cowpox
lessons.mainIdea: In 1796 Edward Jenner showed that cowpox could protect a person from smallpox, the idea behind the first vaccine.
reading: In the 1700s, smallpox killed many people in every part of the world. Those who lived often had deep scars. In the English countryside, people noticed something strange. Milkmaids who had caught cowpox, a mild disease from cows, seemed not to catch smallpox.

Edward Jenner was a country doctor who took this story seriously. In 1796 he took material from a cowpox sore on the hand of a milkmaid named Sarah Nelmes. He put it into small cuts on the arm of a boy named James Phipps. Later he exposed the boy to smallpox. The boy did not get sick. Tests like this on a child would not be allowed today.

His method came to be called *vaccination*, from the Latin word vacca, meaning cow. A *vaccine* trains the body to fight a disease before a real attack comes. Over the next two centuries, vaccination spread worldwide. In 1980 the World Health Organization declared smallpox gone from the earth.

words.d: a medicine that trains the body's defenses to fight a disease before it attacks
giving a vaccine; Jenner's word, from the Latin vacca, meaning cow
a deadly disease that caused fever and blisters; declared gone from the world in 1980

look.title: Jenner Reports His Work
look.text: Jenner described how people who had caught cowpox from cows seemed protected afterward from smallpox, and he reported the cases he had tested, including the boy James Phipps.
look.cite: Edward Jenner, An Inquiry into the Causes and Effects of the Variolae Vaccinae, 1798
look.prompt: Jenner started from something farm people had noticed. Why was it important that he then tested the idea?

check.q: What did milkmaids who had caught cowpox seem to avoid?
check.why: People noticed that milkmaids who had cowpox did not seem to catch smallpox, and Jenner tested that idea.

check.q: Where does the word vaccine come from?
choices: The name of a London street
check.why: Vaccine comes from the Latin vacca, meaning cow, because Jenner used cowpox.

check.q: When did the World Health Organization declare smallpox gone?
check.why: In 1980 the World Health Organization declared smallpox eradicated.

lessons.title: Semmelweis and Clean Hands
lessons.mainIdea: In 1847 Ignaz Semmelweis showed that doctors washing their hands saved the lives of new mothers.
reading: In the 1840s, the Vienna General Hospital in Austria had two clinics where babies were born. In one, doctors and medical students helped mothers. In the other, midwives did. Many more mothers died of a fever after birth in the doctors' clinic. Families knew it and begged not to go there.

Dr. Ignaz Semmelweis wanted to know why. He noticed that doctors often came straight from studying the bodies of people who had died. Then a fellow doctor cut his finger during such a study and died of an illness like the mothers' fever. Semmelweis guessed that the doctors' hands carried something deadly.

In 1847 he made doctors wash their hands in a chlorine solution before seeing mothers. Deaths in his clinic fell sharply. Yet many doctors refused to believe him, and he could not explain what the harmful matter was. Today *hand hygiene* is one of the most important ways to stop *infection* in any hospital.

words.d: an illness caused when germs get into the body and grow
cleaning hands with soap and water or hand rub to remove germs

look.title: Two Clinics, One Difference
look.text: Picture two rooms in the same hospital. The same kind of mothers arrive in both. In one room, the helpers come in from studying the dead. In the other room, they do not. Far more mothers die in the first room.
look.prompt: What one difference did Semmelweis focus on? How did changing only that one thing make his test fair?

check.q: What did Semmelweis ask doctors to do in 1847?
choices: Open the windows to let out bad air
Wash their hands in a chlorine solution
check.why: Semmelweis had doctors wash their hands in chlorine solution before seeing mothers.

check.q: Why did more mothers die in the doctors' clinic?
choices: Doctors carried harmful matter on their hands from studying the dead
The midwives' clinic had better food
Mothers in that clinic were older
check.why: Semmelweis noticed doctors came from studying bodies and guessed their hands carried something deadly.

check.q: Why did many doctors at first reject his idea?
choices: He could not explain what the harmful matter was
He had no clinic of his own
He worked in London, not Vienna
check.why: Semmelweis's results were strong, but he could not yet explain the cause, and many doctors refused to believe him.

lessons.title: Surgery Without Pain
lessons.mainIdea: In 1846 a public operation in Boston showed that ether could put a patient to sleep so surgery caused no pain.
reading: Before the 1840s, surgery was a terrible ordeal. Patients were awake. Strong helpers held them down. Surgeons worked as fast as they could, sometimes in a minute or two, because the pain was so great. Many people chose to suffer with an illness rather than face the knife.

On October 16, 1846, at Massachusetts General Hospital in Boston, a dentist named William Morton gave a patient ether vapor to breathe. The patient fell into a deep sleep. The surgeon removed a growth from his neck. When the patient woke, he said he had felt no real pain. The room where it happened is now called the Ether Dome.

This was a public demonstration of *anesthesia*, a way to block pain during treatment. News spread quickly to Europe. Soon chloroform was used too. Anesthesia let surgeons work slowly and carefully. Today a doctor called an *anesthesiologist* watches the patient's breathing and heart the whole time.

words.d: medicine that blocks pain, often by putting a patient into a sleep-like state, during treatment
a doctor who gives anesthesia and watches the patient during surgery

look.title: A Slow, Careful Surgeon
look.text: Imagine two surgeons. One must finish in two minutes while the patient screams. The other can take an hour, check each step and stop to think, because the patient is asleep.
look.prompt: Which surgeon can do more delicate work? Explain how anesthesia changed what surgery could do.

check.q: Where was ether publicly shown to prevent pain in surgery in 1846?
check.why: The 1846 ether demonstration took place at Massachusetts General Hospital, in the room now called the Ether Dome.

check.q: Why did surgeons before anesthesia work very fast?
choices: Germs had not yet been discovered
Light was too dim to see
Patients were awake and in great pain
check.why: Without anesthesia patients felt everything, so surgeons worked as fast as they could.

check.q: What does an anesthesiologist do?
choices: Gives anesthesia and watches the patient during surgery
check.why: An anesthesiologist is the doctor who gives anesthesia and watches breathing and heart during surgery.

lessons.title: Snow's Map
lessons.mainIdea: John Snow mapped cholera deaths in 1854 and traced them to one water pump on Broad Street.
reading: In 1854 most people believed cholera spread through miasma, a bad smell rising from filth. John Snow thought cholera spread through dirty water. When cholera hit Soho, London, he had a chance to test his idea.

Snow marked each death on a street map. The marks crowded around the Broad Street pump. He also looked for cases that did not fit. A woman who lived far away had died, but she had the water brought from Broad Street because she liked its taste. Brewery workers nearby drank beer and mostly stayed well. These odd cases made his case stronger, not weaker.

Snow also compared two water companies in another part of London. Homes served by a company that drew water from a dirtier part of the River Thames had far more cholera deaths. The water, not the smell, was the link. Years later, other scientists found the cholera germ itself.

words.d: an illness spread through dirty water that causes severe diarrhea and loss of body water
the old idea that disease came from bad-smelling air

look.title: Snow Explains His Case
look.text: Snow wrote that nearly all the deaths had taken place a short distance from the Broad Street pump, and that the people who died far away could often be traced to drinking its water.
look.cite: John Snow, On the Mode of Communication of Cholera, 2nd edition, 1855
look.prompt: Why did Snow pay close attention to the deaths that happened far from the pump?

check.q: What did most people in 1854 believe caused cholera?
check.why: Most people then blamed miasma, a bad smell in the air; Snow challenged that idea.

check.q: Why did the brewery workers support Snow's idea?
choices: They lived far from Broad Street
They all drank from the pump and died
They drank beer made on site and mostly stayed well
They smelled the bad air every day
check.why: The brewery workers were near the pump but drank beer instead of pump water, and most stayed well.

check.q: What did Snow's study of two water companies show?
choices: Both companies had the same number of deaths
Smell was worse near the cleaner company
Homes with dirtier river water had more cholera deaths
check.why: Homes supplied with water from a dirtier part of the Thames had far more cholera deaths.

lessons.title: The Birth of Epidemiology
lessons.mainIdea: Epidemiology studies who gets sick, where and when, to find causes and stop disease from spreading.
reading: Snow never saw the cholera germ through a microscope. He found the cause by counting cases and looking for patterns in people, places and time. This kind of work is called *epidemiology*. An *epidemic* is an outbreak of disease that spreads to many people in an area at once.

Epidemiologists ask simple questions. Who got sick? Where did they live, work and eat? When did they get sick? What did the sick people share that the healthy people did not? The answers can point to a cause, like a pump, a food or a kind of contact.

Today disease detectives still work this way. In the United States, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention trains people to track outbreaks, such as food poisoning from one restaurant. Like Snow, they draw maps, compare groups and share what they find so leaders can act.

words.d: the study of who gets sick, where and when, in order to find causes and prevent disease
an outbreak of disease that spreads to many people in one area at the same time
a sudden rise in cases of a disease in one place

look.title: The School Lunch Mystery
look.text: Twelve students feel sick on Tuesday afternoon. All twelve ate the chicken salad at lunch. Of the students who ate pizza instead, none felt sick. Students came from different classes and different buses.
look.prompt: Think like an epidemiologist. What do the sick students share? What would you check next?

check.q: What is epidemiology?
choices: The study of who gets sick, where and when
check.why: Epidemiology studies patterns of illness in people, places and time to find causes.

check.q: How did Snow find the cause of the Soho outbreak without seeing a germ?
choices: By counting cases and finding a pattern
By growing germs in a dish
check.why: Snow counted and mapped cases to find a pattern that pointed to the pump.

check.q: Which U.S. agency trains people to track outbreaks today?
choices: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
check.why: The CDC trains disease detectives who track outbreaks in the United States.

lessons.title: Pasteur and Pasteurization
lessons.mainIdea: Louis Pasteur showed that tiny living microbes cause spoiling and disease, and that gentle heating can kill them.
reading: In France in the 1850s and 1860s, wine and beer makers had a problem. Their drinks often went sour. They asked the chemist Louis Pasteur for help. Under a microscope he saw tiny living things, called *microbes*, growing in the spoiled drinks.

Pasteur found that heating the liquid gently, without boiling it, killed many of the harmful microbes. This is *pasteurization*, named after him. Later it was used for milk. Pasteurized milk has prevented a great deal of illness, especially in children.

Many people then believed that life could appear on its own from rotting matter. Pasteur tested this with flasks that had long curved necks. Dust and microbes from the air got stuck in the curve. The broth inside stayed clear. When he broke the neck, microbes got in and the broth spoiled. Microbes came from other microbes. This helped build *germ theory*: the idea that germs cause many diseases.

words.d: living things too small to see without a microscope, such as bacteria
heating a liquid gently to kill harmful microbes; named after Louis Pasteur
the idea, proved in the 1800s, that tiny germs cause many diseases

look.title: The Swan-Neck Flask
look.text: Two flasks hold the same boiled broth. One has a long, curved neck open to the air. The other has its neck broken off. Days later, the broken one is cloudy. The curved one is still clear.
look.prompt: Both flasks touch air. What is the one difference, and what does it tell you about where microbes come from?

check.q: What does pasteurization do?
choices: Gently heats a liquid to kill harmful microbes
check.why: Pasteurization gently heats a liquid, without boiling, to kill many harmful microbes.

check.q: Why did the broth in the curved-neck flask stay clear?
choices: Dust and microbes got trapped in the curve
It had no air at all
check.why: The curve trapped dust and microbes from the air, so none reached the broth.

check.q: What is germ theory?
choices: The idea that bad smells cause disease
The idea that tiny germs cause many diseases
The idea that life appears from rotting matter
The idea that cows cause smallpox
check.why: Germ theory says tiny living germs cause many diseases.

lessons.title: Pasteur and Rabies
lessons.mainIdea: In 1885 Pasteur's team gave a rabies vaccine to a bitten boy, Joseph Meister, who survived.
reading: Rabies is a disease spread by the bite of an infected animal, such as a dog, bat or raccoon. Once signs of rabies appear, it is almost always deadly. In the 1800s, people feared mad dogs for good reason.

Pasteur's team made a weakened form of the rabies germ from the spinal cords of infected rabbits, dried for different lengths of time. In July 1885, a mother brought her nine-year-old son, Joseph Meister, to Paris. A rabid dog had bitten him many times. The team gave him a series of shots over about ten days. He never developed rabies.

Rabies moves slowly from a bite toward the brain. That gives a vaccine time to work after the bite. This is still true today. If a person is bitten by an animal that might have rabies, doctors give shots right away. Anyone bitten by an animal should tell a trusted adult and see a doctor.

words.d: a disease spread by animal bites that attacks the brain; shots right after a bite prevent it
a germ made less harmful so it can train the body's defenses without causing illness

look.title: Chance and the Prepared Mind
look.text: Pasteur told listeners that in science, lucky chances help only those whose minds are already prepared to notice them.
look.cite: Louis Pasteur, lecture at the University of Lille, 1854
look.prompt: How do Jenner and Snow show this idea at work? Give one example.

check.q: Who was Joseph Meister?
choices: The surgeon at the Ether Dome
A boy bitten by a rabid dog who received Pasteur's vaccine in 1885
A brewery worker on Broad Street
check.why: Joseph Meister, age nine, was the bitten boy who received Pasteur's rabies vaccine and survived.

check.q: Why can a rabies vaccine work even after a bite?
choices: Rabies moves slowly from the bite toward the brain
check.why: Rabies travels slowly toward the brain, which gives the vaccine time to work.

check.q: What should a person do after being bitten by an animal that might have rabies?
choices: Tell a trusted adult and see a doctor right away
Wait to see if signs appear
Wash it and forget about it
check.why: Doctors give rabies shots right after a possible exposure, so seeing a doctor quickly matters.

lessons.title: Koch Finds the Germs
lessons.mainIdea: Robert Koch proved that specific bacteria cause specific diseases, finding the tuberculosis germ in 1882.
reading: Robert Koch was a German country doctor who turned his home into a lab. He learned to grow bacteria in pure form and to stain them with dyes so they showed up clearly under a microscope. *Bacteria* are one-celled living things; most are harmless, but some cause disease.

In 1882 Koch announced that he had found the bacterium that causes *tuberculosis*, a lung disease that was then one of the leading causes of death in Europe. He announced it on March 24. That date is now World Tuberculosis Day. In 1883 and 1884, working in Egypt and India, his team identified the cholera bacterium, backing up what Snow's maps had shown.

Koch also set out steps to prove a germ causes a disease. Find the germ in every sick person. Grow it pure. Give it to a healthy animal and see the same disease. Find the same germ again. These steps, called Koch's postulates, turned germ theory into careful science.

words.d: one-celled living things; most are harmless or helpful, and some cause disease
a disease caused by bacteria that usually attacks the lungs
Koch's steps for proving that a certain germ causes a certain disease

look.title: Germs Named in the 1800s
look.cite: Dates as given in standard histories of medicine, e.g. Roy Porter, The Greatest Benefit to Mankind, 1997
look.prompt: How many years passed between Snow's 1854 map and the cholera germ being identified? What does that gap show?

check.q: What did Koch find in 1882?
check.why: In 1882 Koch announced the tuberculosis bacterium; March 24 is now World Tuberculosis Day.

check.q: How did Koch's cholera work connect to John Snow?
choices: It showed cholera spread by bad air
It found the germ that explained Snow's water evidence
check.why: Koch's team identified the cholera bacterium, backing up Snow's evidence that water carried the disease.

check.q: Which is one of Koch's postulates?
choices: Blame the smell of the air
Grow the germ in pure form
check.why: Koch's steps included growing the germ pure and showing it causes the same disease in a healthy animal.

lessons.title: Lister and Antiseptics
lessons.mainIdea: In 1867 Joseph Lister used carbolic acid to kill germs in wounds, and far fewer surgery patients died of infection.
reading: Anesthesia made surgery painless, but many patients still died afterward. Their wounds filled with pus and infection. Surgeons wore old coats stiff with blood and did not wash their tools between patients. In Glasgow, Scotland, a surgeon named Joseph Lister read Pasteur's work on microbes and had an idea.

If microbes spoiled broth, perhaps microbes also infected wounds. Lister began using carbolic acid, a chemical already used to treat sewage, to clean wounds, dressings and tools. He tried it on broken bones where the bone had pierced the skin, a kind of injury that often turned deadly.

In 1867 he reported that his patients healed far better. He called his method *antiseptic* surgery. An antiseptic is a chemical that kills germs on skin or wounds. Later surgeons went further with *aseptic* surgery: keeping germs out from the start with sterile gowns, gloves and tools.

words.d: a substance that kills germs on skin, wounds or tools
free of germs; aseptic surgery keeps germs out from the start
completely free of living germs

look.title: Lister's Report
look.text: Lister explained that, since Pasteur had shown that microbes cause decay, wounds could be kept from festering by destroying the germs with a substance such as carbolic acid.
look.cite: Joseph Lister, On the Antiseptic Principle in the Practice of Surgery, The Lancet, 1867
look.prompt: How did Lister use another scientist's discovery to solve a problem in his own field?

check.q: What chemical did Lister use to kill germs in wounds?
check.why: Lister used carbolic acid on wounds, dressings and tools.

check.q: Whose work gave Lister the idea that microbes infected wounds?
check.why: Lister read Pasteur's work showing that microbes cause spoiling and applied it to wounds.

check.q: How is aseptic surgery different from antiseptic surgery?
choices: It kills germs only after surgery ends
It keeps germs out from the start with sterile tools and gowns
check.why: Antiseptic surgery kills germs present; aseptic surgery keeps germs from getting in at all.

lessons.title: How the Big Idea Changed
lessons.mainIdea: Across the 1800s, evidence slowly replaced the miasma idea with germ theory, and that changed daily life.
reading: For centuries, many doctors believed disease came from bad air or from an imbalance of body fluids. These ideas were not silly. Filthy places really did have more disease. But the true cause was usually germs living in the filth, water or food.

The change came piece by piece. Jenner showed that protection could be trained. Semmelweis showed that hands carried danger. Snow showed that water spread cholera. Pasteur showed that microbes came from other microbes. Koch proved which germ caused which disease. Lister showed that killing germs saved lives. No single person did it alone.

Germ theory changed everyday life. Cities built clean water systems and sewers. Hospitals began to scrub and sterilize. Families learned to wash hands, cook food well and keep milk cold. Much of what feels like common sense today began with these tests. Science changed its mind because the evidence was strong.

words.d: facts and observations that show whether an idea is true
an underground pipe that carries waste water away from homes

look.title: Steps Toward Germ Theory
rows: Snow and the Broad Street pump
look.cite: Dates as given in standard histories of medicine, e.g. Roy Porter, The Greatest Benefit to Mankind, 1997
look.prompt: Which of these steps came before anyone had proved that germs cause disease? What does that tell you about good evidence?

check.q: Why did the miasma idea seem reasonable to people long ago?
choices: Microscopes showed germs in the air
Vaccines were made from bad air
Filthy places really did have more disease
check.why: Dirty places did have more disease, but the real cause was usually germs in the filth, water or food.

check.q: Which statement best describes how germ theory was accepted?
choices: Many people's tests added up over time

check.why: Jenner, Semmelweis, Snow, Pasteur, Koch and Lister each added evidence over many years.

check.q: Which everyday habit grew out of germ theory?
choices: Avoiding bad smells to stay healthy
Washing hands and keeping milk cold
Carrying flowers to clean the air
Doing surgery as fast as possible
check.why: Germ theory led families to wash hands, cook food well and keep milk cold.

review.q: What did John Snow do at the Broad Street pump in 1854?
choices: Found the cholera germ with a microscope
Convinced leaders to remove the pump handle
review.why: Snow's evidence led local leaders to remove the handle of the Broad Street pump.
Joseph Lister introduced antiseptic surgery with carbolic acid in 1867.

review.q: What did Semmelweis and Lister both try to stop?
review.why: Semmelweis used handwashing and Lister used antiseptics, both to stop germs reaching patients.

review.q: Why is Snow called a father of epidemiology?
choices: He grew the first pure bacteria
He found a cause by mapping and counting cases
review.why: Snow tracked who got sick and where, the core method of epidemiology.

review.q: What made Jenner's method work against smallpox?
choices: Cowpox killed smallpox germs in the air
Cowpox trained the body to resist smallpox
review.why: Cowpox was mild but trained the body's defenses to resist smallpox.

review.q: What did the 1846 Boston demonstration show?
review.why: At Massachusetts General Hospital, ether put a patient to sleep so he felt no real pain.

review.q: What did Pasteur's curved-neck flasks show?
choices: Microbes come from other microbes, not from nothing
review.why: The broth stayed clear when microbes were trapped, showing life did not appear on its own.

review.q: How did Koch strengthen germ theory?
choices: He mapped cholera deaths in London
He set steps to prove a certain germ causes a certain disease
He made doctors wash with chlorine
review.why: Koch's postulates gave clear steps to prove that a specific germ causes a specific disease.

chapters.title: Antibiotics and the 1900s
chapters.bigQuestion: How did new discoveries and public health work help people in the 1900s live much longer lives?

story.title: The Moldy Dish
story.kicker: A scientist comes home from vacation and notices what is not growing.
paragraphs: In September 1928, Alexander Fleming came back to his lab at St. Mary's Hospital in London after a summer vacation. Fleming studied bacteria. Before he left, he had stacked glass dishes of bacteria on his bench. Now he began sorting them to clean up.

One dish looked spoiled. A fuzzy blue-green mold had grown on it. Many scientists would have tossed it out. But Fleming looked closer. All around the mold was a clear ring. The bacteria that covered the rest of the dish had not grown there.

Something from the mold was stopping the bacteria. Fleming grew more of the mold, a kind of Penicillium, and tested the juice it made. It stopped many kinds of harmful bacteria. He named the substance penicillin and reported it in 1929.

Fleming could not make enough pure penicillin to treat patients. That took another team more than ten years, and a war, and help from a lab in Peoria, Illinois. But it all began because one scientist noticed a clear ring on a dish that looked like a mistake.
story.think: Fleming noticed what was not there. Why can an unexpected result be as useful as an expected one?

sections.title: New Ways to See and Treat

lessons.title: X-Rays Show the Inside
lessons.mainIdea: In 1895 Wilhelm Röntgen discovered X-rays, which let doctors see bones inside the body without surgery.
reading: In November 1895, the German physicist Wilhelm Röntgen was testing electric current in a glass tube in a darkened room. He noticed that a screen across the room began to glow. Some unknown ray was passing through the air, and even through paper and wood. He called it the X-ray, because X stands for something unknown.

Röntgen found that the rays passed through skin and muscle but were blocked by bone. He made an image of his wife's hand that showed her bones and her ring. Within months, doctors around the world were using *X-rays* to find broken bones and swallowed objects.

Early users did not know that strong doses of X-rays could harm the body. Some workers were hurt. Today *radiology* uses much smaller doses, and staff wear shields. Röntgen won the first Nobel Prize in Physics in 1901. X-rays opened the door to later imaging such as CT scans.

words.d: invisible rays that pass through soft tissue but are blocked by bone, used to make pictures of the inside of the body
the branch of medicine that uses images such as X-rays to find and treat problems

look.title: A Picture Without a Cut
look.text: A girl falls off her bike and her wrist swells. Before 1895, a doctor could only feel the wrist and guess. Now a technician places her hand on a plate, steps behind a shield and takes an image. The doctor sees a thin crack in one bone.
look.prompt: How does seeing the crack change what the doctor can do? What did doctors have to do before X-rays?

check.q: Why did Röntgen call his discovery the X-ray?
choices: It was shaped like an X
It came from a star named X
check.why: Röntgen used X, the sign for an unknown, because he did not know what the rays were.

check.q: What part of the body blocks X-rays and shows up clearly?
check.why: X-rays pass through skin and muscle but are blocked by bone.

check.q: Why do X-ray staff wear shields today?
choices: Strong doses of X-rays can harm the body
check.why: Early workers were hurt by strong doses, so today doses are small and staff use shields.

lessons.title: Insulin for Diabetes
lessons.mainIdea: In 1921–22, Frederick Banting and Charles Best in Toronto helped discover insulin, which let people with type 1 diabetes live.
reading: Before the 1920s, a child with type 1 diabetes usually lived only a short time. In *diabetes*, the body cannot control the sugar in the blood. In type 1, the pancreas, an organ near the stomach, stops making enough of a hormone called *insulin*. Without insulin, the body cannot use sugar for energy.

In 1921, at the University of Toronto in Canada, Frederick Banting and his student helper Charles Best took insulin from the pancreas of dogs. Chemist James Collip helped purify it, in a lab led by John Macleod. In January 1922, a fourteen-year-old boy named Leonard Thompson received insulin and grew stronger.

Insulin does not cure diabetes. It is a treatment a person needs every day. But it turned a deadly illness into one people can live with for a long, full life. Today many people with diabetes check their blood sugar and take insulin with help from their doctor and care team.

words.d: a condition in which the body cannot control the amount of sugar in the blood
a hormone made by the pancreas that lets the body use sugar for energy
a chemical messenger made in the body that tells organs what to do

look.title: Treatment or Cure?
look.text: A cure makes a disease go away for good. A treatment manages a disease so a person can live well. Glasses do not cure blurry vision, but they let a person see clearly every day. Insulin works in a similar way for type 1 diabetes.
look.prompt: Is insulin a cure or a treatment? Use the glasses example to explain your answer.

check.q: Where was insulin first used to treat a patient in 1922?
check.why: The insulin work took place at the University of Toronto, where Leonard Thompson was treated in 1922.

check.q: What happens in type 1 diabetes?
choices: The pancreas does not make enough insulin
check.why: In type 1 diabetes the pancreas stops making enough insulin to use sugar for energy.

check.q: Why is insulin called a treatment and not a cure?
choices: It makes diabetes go away forever
People need it every day to manage diabetes
check.why: Insulin manages diabetes when taken regularly, but it does not make the condition go away.

lessons.title: Fleming's Discovery
lessons.mainIdea: In 1928 Alexander Fleming noticed that a mold made a substance, penicillin, that stopped bacteria from growing.
reading: Before antibiotics, a small cut, a sore throat or an ear infection could turn deadly if bacteria spread. Doctors had few ways to stop an infection once it began. Pneumonia, a lung infection, killed many adults and children.

In 1928, Alexander Fleming found a clear ring around a mold in a dish of bacteria. The mold was a kind of Penicillium. Its juice stopped many bacteria from growing. Fleming called the substance *penicillin*. It was the first *antibiotic* of its kind: a medicine that kills bacteria or stops them from growing.

Antibiotics work on bacteria. They do not work on viruses, such as the viruses that cause colds and flu. That is why a doctor may not give antibiotics for a cold. Taking the right medicine for the right germ, as a doctor directs, matters.

words.d: a medicine that kills bacteria or stops them from growing; it does not work on viruses
an antibiotic first found in a mold by Alexander Fleming in 1928
a tiny germ, much smaller than bacteria, that causes illnesses such as colds and flu

look.title: Fleming's Report
look.text: Fleming reported that a mold growing on a dish of bacteria had made the colonies around it fade away, and that broth from the mold could stop the growth of many kinds of bacteria.
look.cite: Alexander Fleming, On the Antibacterial Action of Cultures of a Penicillium, British Journal of Experimental Pathology, 1929
look.prompt: What did Fleming observe, and what test did he do next to learn more?

check.q: What did Fleming notice around the mold on his dish?
choices: A clear ring where bacteria did not grow
A thick layer of extra bacteria
A crack like a broken bone
check.why: Fleming saw a clear ring around the mold where bacteria had not grown.

check.q: Which illness will antibiotics NOT treat?
choices: A cold caused by a virus
check.why: Antibiotics work on bacteria, not viruses such as those that cause colds.

check.q: What is an antibiotic?
choices: A medicine that kills bacteria or stops their growth
check.why: An antibiotic kills bacteria or stops them from growing.

lessons.title: Penicillin Goes to War
lessons.mainIdea: During World War II, scientists in Britain and the United States learned to make penicillin in huge amounts.
reading: For about ten years, penicillin stayed a curiosity. It was hard to make and hard to purify. Around 1939, a team at Oxford University in England, led by Howard Florey and Ernst Chain, with Norman Heatley, began to purify it and test it. In mice, it stopped deadly infections. Early patients improved.

World War II made the need urgent, because wounded soldiers often died of infection. Florey and Heatley flew to the United States in 1941 for help. At a government lab in Peoria, Illinois, scientists grew the mold in large tanks. A mold found on a cantaloupe from a Peoria market turned out to make much more penicillin.

Drug companies scaled up *mass production*. By the D-Day landings in 1944, large supplies were ready for Allied troops. After the war, penicillin became common for everyone. Fleming, Florey and Chain shared the Nobel Prize in 1945.

words.d: making a product in very large amounts, often in factories
to separate a substance from everything mixed with it

look.title: From Dish to Factory
look.text: Step 1: a scientist notices a mold in a dish. Step 2: a team purifies the substance and tests it on mice. Step 3: doctors try it on a few patients. Step 4: labs find a better mold and grow it in huge tanks. Step 5: factories make enough for millions.
look.prompt: Which step do you think was hardest? Why did it take many people, not one, to bring penicillin to patients?

check.q: Which Illinois city helped with penicillin production?
check.why: A government lab in Peoria grew the mold in tanks, and a mold from a Peoria market cantaloupe made much more penicillin.

check.q: Why did World War II make penicillin urgent?
choices: Wounded soldiers often died of infection
check.why: Many wounded soldiers died from infected wounds, so large supplies of penicillin were needed.

check.q: Who led the Oxford team that purified penicillin?
check.why: Howard Florey and Ernst Chain, with Norman Heatley, purified and tested penicillin at Oxford.

lessons.title: When Bacteria Fight Back
lessons.mainIdea: Bacteria can become resistant to antibiotics, so these medicines must be used only when needed and as directed.
reading: Bacteria reproduce very fast. When an antibiotic is used, most of the bacteria die. But a few may have a small change that lets them survive. Those survivors multiply. Over time, a whole population of bacteria can become hard to kill. This is *antibiotic resistance*.

Fleming warned about this in his Nobel lecture in 1945. He saw that using too little penicillin could help bacteria learn to resist it. Today, some infections, such as certain staph infections called MRSA, do not respond to common antibiotics. Doctors must use stronger or different medicines.

Everyone can help. Use antibiotics only when a doctor prescribes them. Take them exactly as directed. Never share them or use old leftovers. Do not expect antibiotics for a cold. Good handwashing and vaccines also help, because fewer infections mean fewer antibiotics are needed.

words.d: when bacteria change so that an antibiotic no longer kills them
when a doctor officially orders a medicine for a patient

look.title: The Survivors
look.text: Picture a dish with 1,000 bacteria. An antibiotic kills 999. One has a small change that lets it survive. By next week, it has made millions of copies, and every copy carries the same change.
look.prompt: Will the same antibiotic work on the new millions? Explain how resistance grows.

check.q: What is antibiotic resistance?
choices: Bacteria changing so an antibiotic no longer kills them
check.why: Resistance means bacteria have changed so an antibiotic no longer works against them.

check.q: Who warned about resistance in 1945?
check.why: Fleming warned in his 1945 Nobel lecture that misuse of penicillin could let bacteria resist it.

check.q: Which habit helps slow resistance?
choices: Taking antibiotics only as a doctor directs
Asking for antibiotics for every cold
check.why: Using antibiotics only when prescribed and as directed helps slow resistance.

lessons.title: Salk's Polio Vaccine
lessons.mainIdea: In 1955 Jonas Salk's polio vaccine was declared safe and effective, and polio cases in the U.S. soon fell sharply.
reading: In the early 1950s, summer brought fear to American families. *Polio*, a disease caused by a virus, could weaken muscles, sometimes for life. Some people needed a machine called an iron lung to breathe. Pools and movie theaters sometimes closed. The worst year in the United States was 1952.

Jonas Salk, a scientist at the University of Pittsburgh, made a vaccine from polio virus that had been killed. In 1954, more than a million children took part in a huge test, called a *field trial*. On April 12, 1955, researchers announced that the vaccine was safe and worked well.

Vaccination began right away. Salk did not patent the vaccine. Later, Albert Sabin made a vaccine taken by mouth. Cases in the United States dropped quickly. Today polio has been eliminated from most of the world, and vaccination continues.

words.d: a disease caused by a virus that can weaken or paralyze muscles; prevented by vaccine
a large test of a medicine or vaccine in many people, compared with a group who did not get it

look.title: Polio Cases in the United States
look.cite: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, national polio surveillance data (rounded)
look.prompt: About how many times fewer cases were there in 1965 than in 1952? What changed in between?

check.q: What kind of vaccine did Jonas Salk make?
choices: A vaccine made from killed polio virus
check.why: Salk's vaccine used polio virus that had been killed.

check.q: What happened on April 12, 1955?
choices: Researchers announced the polio vaccine was safe and worked
Insulin was given to a boy
check.why: On April 12, 1955, the results of the field trial were announced.

check.q: Why was the 1954 field trial important?
choices: It found the polio virus under a microscope
It built the first iron lung
It tested the vaccine in more than a million children
check.why: The field trial tested the vaccine on a very large group to show it was safe and effective.

lessons.title: The Shape of DNA
lessons.mainIdea: In 1953 scientists worked out that DNA is a double helix, which explains how living things pass on instructions.
reading: Every living cell carries instructions for how to grow and work. Those instructions are stored in *DNA*. By the 1950s, scientists knew DNA was important, but not what it looked like.

In London, Rosalind Franklin used X-rays to take very sharp pictures of DNA. One image, called Photo 51, showed an X-shaped pattern. Maurice Wilkins, who worked in the same lab, showed it to James Watson. In Cambridge, Watson and Francis Crick used it and other data to build a model. In 1953 they published it: a *double helix*, like a twisted ladder.

The shape explained how DNA copies itself. The two sides unzip, and each side builds a new partner. Watson, Crick and Wilkins received the Nobel Prize in 1962. Franklin had died in 1958, and the prize is not given after death. Many historians now stress that her work was key.

words.d: the molecule in cells that carries the instructions for how a living thing grows and works
the shape of DNA: two strands twisted around each other, like a twisted ladder

look.title: The Twisted Ladder
look.text: Picture a ladder. Now twist it gently so it spirals. The two long sides are the backbones of DNA. The rungs are pairs of chemical letters. When the ladder splits down the middle, each half can build a matching new half.
look.prompt: Why would a shape that can split and rebuild be useful for a cell that divides into two cells?

check.q: Whose X-ray photo helped reveal the shape of DNA?
check.why: Rosalind Franklin's X-ray image, Photo 51, helped Watson and Crick build their model.

check.q: What shape is DNA?
choices: A double helix, like a twisted ladder
check.why: In 1953 Watson and Crick described DNA as a double helix.

check.q: Why did Franklin not share the 1962 Nobel Prize?
choices: She worked in medicine, not science
She had died, and the prize is not given after death
check.why: Franklin died in 1958, and the Nobel Prize is not awarded after death.

lessons.title: Clean Water and Sewers
lessons.mainIdea: Clean drinking water and sewers prevented huge numbers of deaths from diseases such as cholera and typhoid.
reading: Germ theory showed that dirty water spreads disease. Cities acted on that knowledge. They built sewers to carry waste away and treated drinking water to kill germs. Adding chlorine to drinking water began in the United States in the early 1900s. Cases of typhoid, another disease spread by dirty water, fell sharply.

Chicago faced a special problem. The city took its drinking water from Lake Michigan, and its sewage flowed into the Chicago River and then into the lake. In 1900 the city opened the Sanitary and Ship Canal, which reversed the river's flow so sewage moved away from the lake.

This kind of work is *public health*: protecting the health of whole communities, not just treating one patient at a time. Clean water, safe waste removal and *sanitation* may be the biggest life-savers of the 1900s. Many places in the world are still building these systems today.

words.d: work that protects the health of whole communities, such as clean water and vaccines
safe removal of sewage and waste to keep germs away from people
a serious illness caused by bacteria spread through dirty water or food

look.title: One Doctor or One Pipe?
look.text: A doctor can treat one sick child at a time. A clean water pipe reaches every home on the street, every day, before anyone gets sick.
look.prompt: Which one do you think saves more lives over many years? Explain using the idea of public health.

check.q: What did Chicago's Sanitary and Ship Canal do in 1900?
choices: Brought ocean water to the city
Reversed the river so sewage moved away from Lake Michigan
check.why: The canal reversed the Chicago River's flow to keep sewage out of the lake, the city's drinking water.

check.q: What is public health?
choices: Protecting the health of whole communities
Health care only for rich families
check.why: Public health protects whole communities, for example through clean water and vaccines.

check.q: Which disease fell sharply when cities treated drinking water?
check.why: Typhoid spreads through dirty water, so chlorinated water made cases fall.

lessons.title: Safe Food and Medicine
lessons.mainIdea: In 1906 the United States passed its first national food and drug safety laws after reports about unsafe food.
reading: In the early 1900s, some food sold in the United States was spoiled or mislabeled. Some medicines made false promises and did not list what was in them. In 1906 the writer Upton Sinclair published a novel, The Jungle, set in Chicago's meatpacking plants. It described filthy conditions, and readers were shocked.

That same year, Congress passed the Pure Food and Drug Act and the Meat Inspection Act. For the first time, the national government checked meat and required truthful labels on food and medicine. This work grew into today's *Food and Drug Administration*, or FDA.

*Food safety* also means habits at home. Pasteurized milk, refrigerators, washing hands and cooking meat all the way through help keep germs out. When people read a label, check a date or keep leftovers cold, they are using ideas that grew out of germ theory.

words.d: ways of handling, cooking and storing food to prevent illness
the U.S. government agency, called the FDA, that checks the safety of food and medicines

look.title: The Pure Food and Drug Act
look.text: The law made it illegal to make or sell food, drinks or medicines that were impure or falsely labeled, and it required certain ingredients to be listed on the label.
look.cite: Pure Food and Drug Act, United States Congress, 1906
look.prompt: How does a truthful label help a family stay safe? Give one example.

check.q: Which book about Chicago meatpacking helped lead to food safety laws?
choices: On the Mode of Communication of Cholera
check.why: Upton Sinclair's 1906 novel The Jungle described filthy conditions in Chicago meatpacking plants.

check.q: What did the 1906 Pure Food and Drug Act require?
choices: Truthful labels on food and medicine
check.why: The law banned impure or falsely labeled food and medicine.

check.q: Which is a food safety habit at home?
choices: Eating meat that is still raw inside
check.why: Keeping food cold slows germ growth; the other choices raise the risk of illness.

lessons.title: How Life Expectancy Rose
lessons.mainIdea: Life expectancy in the U.S. rose by about thirty years during the 1900s, mostly because fewer children died young.
reading: *Life expectancy* is the average number of years a newborn baby is expected to live. In the United States in 1900, it was about 47 years. By 2000, it was about 77. That is a rise of about thirty years in one century.

This does not mean most adults in 1900 died at 47. Many lived into their 60s and 70s. The average was low because so many babies and young children died of infections, such as diarrhea from dirty water or milk, measles and pneumonia. When fewer children die, the average rises a lot.

What caused the rise? Clean water, sewers and safe food came first. Then vaccines and antibiotics. Better nutrition, housing and medical care also helped. Scientists still discuss how much each one added, but most agree that public health played a very large part.

words.d: the average number of years a newborn is expected to live
a single number that sums up a group, found by adding values and dividing by how many there are

look.title: U.S. Life Expectancy at Birth
look.cite: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, National Center for Health Statistics, Health, United States (rounded)
look.prompt: In which 25-year period did life expectancy rise the most? Which discoveries from this chapter came during that time?

check.q: About what was U.S. life expectancy in 1900?
check.why: U.S. life expectancy at birth was about 47 years in 1900.

check.q: Why was the average so low in 1900?
choices: Many babies and young children died of infections
check.why: Many children died young from infections, which pulled the average down.

check.q: What do most scientists agree played a very large part in the rise?
choices: Public health, such as clean water and safe food
check.why: Clean water, sewers and safe food, the work of public health, played a very large part.

review.q: What did Fleming notice on his dish in 1928?
choices: Bacteria did not grow around a mold
review.why: Fleming saw a clear ring around the mold where bacteria had not grown.
Jonas Salk developed the killed-virus polio vaccine announced in 1955.

review.q: Why won't antibiotics help a cold?
choices: Colds are caused by viruses, and antibiotics work on bacteria
Colds are too mild to treat
review.why: Antibiotics act on bacteria, not on the viruses that cause colds.

review.q: What role did Peoria, Illinois, play in medical history?
choices: The first X-ray was taken there
A lab there helped mass-produce penicillin
review.why: A government lab in Peoria grew penicillin mold in tanks and found a high-yield mold on a cantaloupe.

review.q: How are insulin and penicillin different?
choices: Insulin manages diabetes daily; penicillin kills bacteria in an infection
Insulin kills bacteria; penicillin controls blood sugar
review.why: Insulin is a hormone that manages diabetes; penicillin is an antibiotic against bacteria.

review.q: What did Chicago do in 1900 to protect its drinking water?
review.why: The Sanitary and Ship Canal reversed the river so sewage flowed away from the lake.

review.q: What does the rise in U.S. life expectancy from about 47 to about 77 mostly reflect?
choices: Far fewer children dying of infections
review.why: Most of the rise came because fewer babies and children died young.

review.q: How can people help slow antibiotic resistance?
choices: Take antibiotics only as a doctor prescribes
review.why: Using antibiotics only when prescribed and exactly as directed slows resistance.
